elaine: Heads-up — running the generator streaming sample app I noticed a goroutine leak when cancelling context mid-handshake. Repro below.
sam: Ugh, thanks. Is this the sampleapp in examples/generator or the SDK sample?
elaine: SDK sample (go/sdk/examples/generator-stream). Steps: start a stream, simulate auth refresh that returns 401 from next request, cancel ctx while the runtime is doing the initial handshake.
nina: Can you paste the minimal repro? I can try locally.
elaine: Sure, minimal snippet:
```
ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
req := client.GeneratorStreamRequest{Model: "gpt-xyz", Input: "hello"}
stream, err := genClient.Stream(ctx, req)
if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
// we spawn a goroutine that reads tokens
go func() {
  for {
    tok, err := stream.Recv()
    if err != nil { return }
    fmt.Print(tok.Text)
  }
}()
// simulate auth refresh delay; cancel during handshake
time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
cancel()
// wait a bunch, observe goroutines increasing
```
mike: I think the problem is our Stream() starts a background handshake goroutine that doesn't get the canceled ctx if cancellation happens between network calls. It leaves a recv loop pinned.
sam: Hmm — is the public API Stream(ctx, req) already? If so it should respect ctx everywhere. Maybe our internal spawn uses a new context without tie to parent.
elaine: Exactly. The internal code does: go s.doHandshake(); doHandshake() uses a separate contextWithTimeout(context.Background(), 5s) so cancel on caller doesn't stop it immediately.
nina: That's rough. Two UX options to consider:
  1) require ctx in NewStream/Stream and ensure all internal goroutines inherit it (propagate cancel) — best for correctness.
  2) provide a stream.Close() that reliably aborts handshake and recv loop (ergonomic for users who didn't hold ctx).
sam: I prefer (1). Go idiom is to accept context at entry points. Also, for long-lived streams, returning a cancel func from Stream could help callers who forgot to keep ctx.
mike: We should also update sampleapp to show the correct pattern and add a race test that cancels at various handshake points.
elaine: Another wrinkle — auth refresh path: when token refresh triggers mid-stream, we re-init transport which can create a new connection while old handshake goroutine still waiting, doubling goroutines.
nina: That sounds like a state machine bug — we keep old handshake running on old transport instead of failing fast when auth update occurs.
sam: Quick mitigation: on auth refresh event, broadcast a cancel to all in-flight handshakes for that client token. Longer term, ensure handshake uses the caller ctx.
mike: I'll draft a PR: 1) make Stream(ctx, req) enforce propagating ctx to all background tasks, 2) add stream.Close() idempotent abort, 3) update sampleapp and add a test in generator_integration_test.go that cancels mid-handshake.
elaine: Thanks — that should fix the leak. Also can we add a small note in the SDK docs about "Cancellation expectations" so users know to pass ctx from request lifecycle (http handler ctx etc.)?
sam: Yep. Also add a troubleshooting section: "if you see goroutine growth while canceling streams, check for auth refresh races and ensure ctx is propagated".
build-bot: CI: draft PR #4121 opened by @mike: fix(generator): propagate ctx to handshake + add Close() + tests — running unit tests.
elaine: Nice. Assign to eng-runtime and devex for docs updates. If tests pass, let's backport a patch to the last release branch — this could affect customers using sample apps.
nina: I'll help verify with heavy-cancel fuzz locally once PR lands.
sam: Great collaboration. Small ergonomic tweak: consider returning (stream, cancelFunc, err) for quick callers who want an explicit close without managing ctx object.
mike: Noted — I'll prototype that in the PR as an alternative constructor: StreamWithCancel(ctx, req) -> (s, cancel).
elaine: Perfect. Thanks everyone :thumbsup:
__note__: This document is a single Slack thread. Messages are a single continuous string with sender prefixes per agents.md rules.
